content_metadata.description: This video provides an explanation of how solvent polarity influences retention factor in thin-layer chromatography (TLC).

qAndA.question: What does Rf stand for in the context of TLC?

qAndA.answer: A more polar solvent leads to higher Rf values.
qAndA.question: How does a more polar solvent affect the Rf values of compounds on a TLC plate?

qAndA.answer: A more polar solvent competes better with the polar stationary phase, causing compounds to partition more in favor of the mobile phase and travel faster.
qAndA.question: Why does a more polar solvent result in higher Rf values?

qAndA.answer: When an extremely nonpolar solvent is used, the Rf values approach zero because there is little to no partitioning into the mobile phase.
qAndA.question: What happens to the Rf values when an extremely nonpolar solvent is used?

qAndA.answer: Combinations of solvents allow for fine-tuning the polarity of the mobile phase to achieve optimal separation of compounds.
qAndA.question: Why are combinations of solvents often used in TLC?

text_to_speech: another factor affecting the rate at which compounds move on a TLC plate is the solvent used if a more polar solvent is used it will compete better with the polar stationary phase as a result all spots will partition more in favor of the mobile phase will travel faster and will have a higher RF often combinations of solvents are used so the polarity can be adjusted as needed an example of a TLC is shown here let's assume it was developed using a 90/10 mixture of hexane a nonpolar alkane and ethyl acetate a polar ester if the same mixture is developed using a 95/5 mixture instead lower RFS would result since it is a less polar solvent combination a more polar solvents such as 20% of the lacet 8 in hexane would cause the spots to move faster resulting in higher RS if an extremely polar solvent is used such as straight ethyl acetate we might expect an RF of 1 as both spots move at the same rate as the solvent the other extreme example is when a completely nonpolar solvent is used 100% hexane is not polar enough for any partitioning into the mobile phase to occur at all and the spots remain at the starting point to give an RF of 0

timecoded_text_to_speech.text: Another factor affecting the rate at which compounds move on a TLC plate is the solvent used.
If a more polar solvent is used, it will compete better with the polar stationary phase.
As a result, all spots will partition more in favor of the mobile phase,
will travel faster, and will have a higher RF.
Often, combinations of solvents are used so the polarity can be adjusted as needed.
An example of a TLC is shown here.
Let's assume it was developed using a 90-ton mixture of hexane, a non-polar alkane,
If the same mixture was developed using a 95-5 mixture instead,
lower RFs would result since it is a less polar solvent combination.
A more polar solvent such as 20% of the elacitate in hexane would cause the spots to move faster,
If an extremely polar solvent is used, such as straight ethylacitate,
we might expect an RF of 1, as both spots move at the same rate as the solvent.
The other extreme example is when a completely non-polar solvent is used.
100% hexane is not polar enough for any partitioning into the mobile phase to occur at all,
and the spots remain at the starting point to give an RF of 0.
